content: 1. A 2016 review focused on nutritional interventions, employing a narrative review design. A 2019 review by Forbes targeted men with a history of prostate cancer, excluding those with HIV. Similarly, a 2017 review by Gonçalves examined a general adult population, excluding individuals with HIV. Ivanyi (2015) reviewed the effects of orthoses, footwear, and walking aids on the mobility of children and adolescents with spina bifida. Kamitani (2017) conducted an umbrella review, while Kietrys (2018) presented a case series study design. Koepke (2018) reviewed individuals with multiple sclerosis, and Kong (2002) focused on testosterone therapy in HIV-associated wasting syndrome. 2. Larsen (2019) reviewed a general adult population, excluding those with HIV, while Lee (2013) examined adults at risk for or diagnosed with cardiovascular diseases, excluding those with HIV. Maddocks (2013) reviewed neuromuscular electrical stimulation for muscle weakness in adults with advanced diseases. McKay (2018) evaluated mobile phone applications for health behavior change, and Moraes (2018) assessed psychoneuroimmunology-based interventions. Nelson (2014) reviewed osteoarthritis management, and Omura (2012) focused on the patient experience of hemophilia and HIV. 3. Roeh (2019) reviewed the effects of exercise training on depressive symptoms in somatically ill patients. Roll (2018) conducted a concept analysis on health promotion for individuals with intellectual disabilities. Russell (2014) examined the efficacy of nutritional interventions on soccer skills. Tian (2013) reviewed the effects of chromium picolinate supplementation in overweight or obese adults. Vancampfort (2018) explored physical activity correlates in people living with HIV/AIDS. Yahiaoui (2012) noted that the study design was not a systematic review. 4. Across the reviews, many limitations were identified in design, execution, and reporting. None of the systematic reviews were rated as having high credibility using the AMSTAR 2 tool. Eleven reviews were rated as having moderate credibility, five as low credibility, and six as critically low credibility. Reviews with critically low credibility were excluded from the final evidence profiles due to concerns about comprehensiveness and validity. 5. For the HIV umbrella review, 24 studies were eligible for inclusion in the qualitative synthesis and underwent quality scoring. An independent team of nine reviewers used the AMSTAR 2 tool to assess the quality of the systematic reviews. Of the 24 reviews, five were rated as critically low and excluded. Among the remaining 19 reviews, 12 were rated as high quality, two as moderate, and five as low quality. 6. None of the reviews included evidence published in 2019, and very few included evidence from 2017 or 2018. The number of included studies in each review ranged from 5 to 39, with one review on cancer history including 136 studies. 7. Physical activity guidelines relevant to specific subgroups, such as those with HIV, were provided in the evidence profiles. For HIV, 19 reviews were included after exclusions, representing between 5 and 28 studies. Data for each included review are presented in Appendix A. 8. The AMSTAR 2 credibility ratings for systematic reviews on physical activity in individuals with cancer, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes were detailed. For example, reviews on cancer survivors showed moderate evidence that greater physical activity after diagnosis is associated with lower risks of cancer-specific and all-cause mortality in breast and colorectal cancer survivors. Limited evidence suggested an inverse association between physical activity and all-cause mortality in prostate cancer survivors. 9. For hypertension, strong evidence demonstrated that physical activity reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease progression. However, insufficient evidence was available to determine relationships between physical activity and co-morbid conditions, physical function, or health-related quality of life in adults with hypertension. 10. For type 2 diabetes, strong evidence indicated an inverse association between physical activity and cardiovascular mortality risk. However, insufficient evidence was available to determine relationships between physical activity and physical function or health-related quality of life in this population. 11. The reviews highlighted the need for more comprehensive and high-quality evidence to better understand the relationships between physical activity and health outcomes across various chronic conditions.
